1: # Repo Memory: Specification
2: 
3: | | |
4: |---|---|
5: | **Status** | Draft v0.9 (see Revision history) |
6: | **Date** | 2026-09-30 |
7: | **Scope** | Repository-level memory for coding agents. **Release 1: Antigravity. Release 2: Claude Code.** Text marked **[R2]** belongs to Release 2; Release 1 is built so that Release 2 is an adapter, not a rewrite (§18.6). |
8: | **Implementation** | One Go binary, `repo-memory` (§18) |
9: | **Reference repo** | `esp32-app-foundation` (evidence in Appendix A) |
10: | **Supersedes** | `repo-memory-plugin-architecture-analysis.md` (annotated critique kept for the record) |
11: 
12: ---
13: 
14: ## 1. Purpose
15: 
16: An agent starting work on a large, long-lived repository should behave as if it had been on the project from day one. It should know how each part of the system works and why. It should know what invariants must hold and what has already been tried and failed. It should know what a given error usually means and how to verify a change on real hardware.
17: 
18: This specification defines a memory system that provides that knowledge:
19: 
20: - **automatically**, without the working agent spending tokens to record it;
21: - **efficiently**, delivering only what the current task, file, error or action needs;
22: - **accurately**, keeping each fact tied to the code and evidence it depends on;
23: - **completely**, covering every part of the system, including stable parts nobody has touched for months.
24: 
25: ### 1.1 Goals
26: 
27: | # | Goal |
28: |---|---|
29: | G1 | The working agent writes no memory. All capture and distillation is done by a background sidecar. |
30: | G2 | Every subsystem in the repo has memory coverage, whether or not a conversation has discussed it. |
31: | G3 | Knowledge is delivered at the moment of need (task start, file touch, error, risky action), not only on request. |
32: | G4 | A fact stays valid until something it depends on changes. Age and lack of use never retire knowledge. |
33: | G5 | Trust is earned from outcomes (tests, builds, flash logs, merges, human confirmation), never from retrieval frequency or self-rated confidence. |
34: | G6 | Memory is rebuildable. Improving the pipeline and re-running it over the full history improves all past memory. |
35: | G7 | Knowledge that lives in git is human-readable, reviewable per fact, and merge-safe. |
36: | G8 | The system measures its own effectiveness using signals every session produces. |
37: | G9 | Existing artefacts (PA workspaces, ADRs, design specs, commit history) can be ingested without a special migration path. |
38: 
39: ### 1.2 Non-goals
40: 
41: - Generic chat or personal-assistant memory (user preferences across unrelated projects).
42: - Replacing git, the issue tracker or human-facing documentation. Memory can *feed* documentation (§7.3) but doesn't own it.
43: - A graph database, cloud vector store or any server infrastructure.
44: - Autonomous commits to the user's working branches.
45: - Storing what can be derived cheaply from the code at read time (structure, signatures, call graphs).
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 2. Design principles
50: 
51: | # | Principle | Consequence |
52: |---|---|---|
53: | P1 | **Separate working from remembering.** | The main agent only works. Capture uses hooks (no LLM). Distillation happens asynchronously in the sidecar. |
54: | P2 | **Event-sourced knowledge.** | Sessions, commits, human reviews and imported documents are immutable *events*. Knowledge is a *projection* over events and can be recomputed. |
55: | P3 | **Store only what the code can't tell you.** | Memory holds intent, rationale, ruled-out approaches, failure signatures, hardware and library behaviour, verified procedures, conventions and decisions. Structure is read from the code. |
56: | P4 | **The claim is the unit of knowledge.** | Knowledge is stored as small, typed, evidence-backed claims anchored to code. Documents are generated *views* over claims. |
57: | P5 | **Truth from outcomes.** | A claim's status comes from evidence in the trace (tool results, test outcomes, merges, reverts, human statements), not from the agent's prose. Hypotheses remain hypotheses. |
58: | P6 | **Code is the index.** | Entities are derived from the repository. Retrieval is keyed on the code the agent is touching, the errors it sees and the task text, not on embedding similarity over the opening prompt. |
59: | P7 | **Validity follows dependencies.** | Claims are re-checked when their anchored code, library versions, toolchain or config change. Nothing expires with time or disuse. |
60: | P8 | **Push, with a strict budget.** | Hot-path delivery is deterministic, bounded in tokens and deduplicated per session. Only high-trust claims are pushed. |
61: | P9 | **Humans are the highest authority.** | Human statements and reviews are events with the highest trust. The system asks targeted questions to fill rationale gaps. |
62: | P10 | **Harness-agnostic core, thin adapters.** | Pipeline, stores and views are plain files plus SQLite. There is no custom daemon or socket. Antigravity (Release 1) and Claude Code (Release 2) are adapters behind one interface. Delivery is chosen by each harness's declared *capabilities*, never by its name (§18.3). |
63: | P11 | **Never slow the loop.** | Hooks run synchronously and block the agent. Hook scripts only read precomputed files and indexes. All LLM work happens in the tick. |
64: | P12 | **Review gates sharing, not use.** | A developer's own machine uses new claims as soon as they reach `verified`. Review controls what enters the shared repository. |
65: | P13 | **Evidence must be independent of the memory it supports.** | Only tool outcomes and human-authored messages are evidence; agent text never is. Anything a session was shown by memory (its *exposure*) cannot come back as support for the same claim unless a new outcome actually tested it (§6.6). This prevents memory from reinforcing itself through the sessions it informs, including bug-fixer sessions and report conversations. |
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. Terminology
70: 
71: | Term | Meaning |
72: |---|---|
73: | **Session** | One agent conversation, including any subagent sessions it spawned. |
74: | **Raw transcript** | The harness's native record of a session (Antigravity conversation DB, Claude Code JSONL). |
75: | **Episode** | The compacted, scrubbed, harness-neutral record of a session produced by the pipeline (§5.1). |
76: | **Event** | Any immutable input to the knowledge projection: an episode, a commit, a human review decision, a human answer, or an imported document. |
77: | **Entity** | A thing claims are about: a code element (subsystem, file, symbol, config key, build env, topic, MCP tool, error string) or an external element (library@version, SDK version, board, tool). |
78: | **Anchor** | A reference from a claim to an entity, carrying a fingerprint of the anchored content. |
79: | **Claim** | A typed, evidence-backed statement about one or more entities (§5.3). |
80: | **View** | A generated document rendered from claims and entities (§5.5). |
81: | **Claim index** | A generated view listing, per subsystem, each pushable claim's ID and `relevant_when` line, so an agent can find relevant claims itself with ordinary file reads (§5.5). |
82: | **Memory artefact** | A file a working agent or the PA writes to record knowledge (PA `MEMORY.md`, `PROJECT.md` session logs, completion reports, a harness-native memory store). Writes to one are a triage signal (§6.4). |
83: | **Event path** | Work started by a harness hook. Knows exactly which session changed, must return in milliseconds, and only reads, injects and writes spool files (§4.1). |
84: | **Time path** | Work started by a scheduled tick. Does all asynchronous work (§4.1). |
85: | **Sidecar** | An Antigravity-managed scheduled job: a periodic tick, not a daemon. |
86: | **Tick** | One scheduled run of `repo-memory tick`. It advances pending jobs within a time budget, then exits. |
87: | **Job** | A durable unit of asynchronous work in the job table (§4.3), advanced step by step across ticks. |
88: | **Housekeeping run** | A headless `agy -p` call made by the pipeline, on the user's Antigravity quota. Not visible in the IDE (§4.4). |
89: | **Report** | An IDE-visible conversation (`agentapi`) that the tick starts for the human, only when there is something worth reviewing (§4.4). |
90: | **Trigger** | A runtime condition that causes knowledge to be delivered to the working agent (§7). |
91: | **Exposure** | A session receiving memory content: pushed by a hook, returned by a pull tool, or read directly from `.memory/`. Recorded per step in the episode (§5.1) and used to enforce P13. |
92: | **Salience window** | A range of episode steps selected mechanically around failures, fixes, reverts, human decisions and trade-off reasoning. Extraction reads windows rather than whole episodes (§6.4). |
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 4. Architecture overview
97: 
98: ```
99:           EVENT PATH (hooks)                               TIME PATH (scheduled tick, every minute)
100:   ┌──────── Working agent (Antigravity / Claude Code) ─────────┐
101:   │  works normally — writes no memory                         │
102:   │  ▲ push: brief · touch · error · risky action · déjà-vu    │
103:   │  │ pull: ask / why / history / brief / note / stats ───────┼──▶ MCP server ──▶ agy -p (synchronous)
104:   └──┼───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
105:      │ inline        │ Stop · PreInvocation · PreToolUse · PostToolUse
106:      │ (no LLM)      ▼ write spool files only
107:      │        ┌─────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
108:      │        │   spool/    │──────▶ │ Tick: ingest spool → job table → next steps   │
109:      │        └─────────────┘        │  • mechanical work in-process                 │
110:      │                               │  • LLM steps: agy -p child processes          │
111:      │                               │    (headless housekeeping; waited, bounded)   │
112:      │                               │  • reports: agentapi (visible in the IDE)     │
113:      │                               │  • sweep, git checks, calendar jobs           │
114:      │                               └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
115:      │                                                       ▼
116:      │          1 Compact → 2 Triage → 3 Extract → 4 Reconcile → 5 Verify → 6 Publish
117:      │             │                             │                          │
118:      │             ▼                             ▼                          ▼
119:      │     Episode log (private)   Claim store (git) + entity skeleton   Views (generated)
120:      │                                           │                          │
121:      └──────────── alerts/ + local index (SQLite, rebuildable) ◀────────────┘
122: 
123:   Human events: answers in review reports, memory-PR review → highest-trust events
124: ```
125: 
126: ### 4.1 Invocation paths
127: 
128: Nothing runs continuously. Two paths start all work, and each has a strictly separate job:
129: 
130: | | **Event path: hooks** | **Time path: scheduled tick** |
131: |---|---|---|
132: | Fired by | Agent, model, tool and session events in the harness | Cron, every minute (Antigravity plugin sidecar, `builtin: schedule`). **[R2]** On Claude Code, harness-run `async: true` hooks also start it (§12.2). Elsewhere, the OS scheduler running `repo-memory tick`. |
133: | Knows | Exactly which conversation, transcript, workspace and step just changed | Discovers state from the spool, the job table, transcripts and git |
134: | Constraint | Synchronous and blocking the agent loop, so it must finish in milliseconds | A time budget per tick (default 50 s); never overlaps itself (`tick.lock`) |
135: | Does | Reads the index and `alerts/`; injects; writes spool files | All asynchronous work: ingest the spool, advance jobs, run LLM steps, sweep, calendar jobs |
136: | Never | Starts processes, calls a model, uses the network, or writes the job table | Leaves work running after it exits |
137: 
138: **[R2]** On Claude Code, a hook registered with `async: true` is run in the background *by the harness*. That hook's command simply is `repo-memory tick`, so it is another time-path trigger, not a hook doing work, and the tick stays the only executor.
139: 
140: **Rule:** work may outlive a tick only as durable job state. Every executor is either a child process that the tick starts and waits for (with a timeout), or a harness-supervised conversation (reports). Nothing is detached.
141: 
142: **Why harness-level rather than OS-level:**
143: - **Portability.** Nothing depends on per-OS process-detachment behaviour, inherited output pipes, or how each harness supervises hook children.
144: - **Visibility.** Each tick's output lands in `sidecar_data/<id>/logs`, and there is a single job table.
145: - **Simplicity.** There is one place to look for what ran, when, and at what cost.
146: 
147: The cost is that asynchronous LLM results arrive at tick granularity: up to about a minute, plus the call time.
148: 
149: ### 4.2 Invocation map
150: 
151: | Work | Event path | Time path |
152: |---|---|---|
153: | Capture a finished session | `Stop`: write a spool entry and copy the transcript | Sweep catches sessions with no `Stop` (crash, kill, sessions from before install, subagents per E8); promotes idle sessions to processing |
154: | Process episodes (stages 1–6) | none | Jobs advanced each tick within budget |
155: | System map | Loaded by the `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` include | Regenerated when claims change |
156: | Task brief | `PreInvocation` (`invocationNum == 0`) inline from the index. If lexical linking fails, spool a brief request. | Next tick runs it as a housekeeping run; the next `PreInvocation` delivers it. The agent can also call `memory.brief` synchronously. |
157: | Touch, error delivery | `PreInvocation` inline | none |
158: | Risky action | `PreToolUse` gate modes; `PreInvocation` injection (§7.5) | none |
159: | Déjà-vu tier 1 (lexical) | `PreToolUse` on the concrete call; `PreInvocation` on the latest reasoning | none |
160: | Déjà-vu tier 2 (semantic) | `PreInvocation` spools a request when new reasoning mentions an entity with `ruled-out` claims | Next tick checks it; the next `PreInvocation` delivers any alert |
161: | Re-check after a git change by the agent | `PostToolUse` on `run_command`: if the step at `stepIdx` is a merge, checkout, pull, rebase or dependency update, spool a re-check | Tick compares HEAD, lockfile and sdkconfig hashes to catch git operations made outside the agent |
162: | Publish the memory PR | none | Daily |
163: | Review report (§4.4) | none | Weekly, only if there is something to review |
164: | Metrics roll-up, coverage | none | Daily |
165: | Index rebuild | `repo-memory reindex` (manual) | If the index is missing or its schema is outdated |
166: 
167: ### 4.3 Job table
168: 
169: Asynchronous work is tracked in a private SQLite job table (`<data-dir>/<repo-id>/jobs.sqlite`). Hooks never write to it; they write spool files, which the tick ingests. The hot path therefore never waits on a database lock.
170: 
171: | Field | Purpose |
172: |---|---|
173: | `id`, `kind`, `priority` | e.g. `compact`, `triage`, `extract`, `reconcile`, `verify`, `publish`, `brief`, `dejavu`, `recheck`, `report` |
174: | `idempotency_key` | Hash of inputs + stage + pipeline version, so duplicates are no-ops |
175: | `state` | `queued` → `running` → `done`, or `failed` → retried with backoff → `dead` after N attempts. Reports: `submitted(conversation_id)` → `done` when the conversation goes idle. |
176: | `lease_expires`, `attempts`, `next_attempt_at` | Recovery after a crashed or killed tick |
177: | `cost` | Tokens, duration and model, taken from the `agy` JSON output |
178: 
179: **Each tick, in order:**
180: 1. Take `tick.lock`; exit if a previous tick is still running.
181: 2. Ingest spool files as jobs.
182: 3. Reclaim expired leases.
183: 4. Sweep transcripts and check git hashes (cheap, mechanical).
184: 5. Poll report conversations.
185: 6. Run interactive jobs (briefs, déjà-vu) first.
186: 7. Run batch jobs until the time budget is spent, with bounded concurrency (default: 2 `agy -p` children at once).
187: 8. Run due calendar jobs.
188: 9. Exit.
189: 
190: **Concurrency rules.** Extraction runs in parallel. Reconcile and publish are single-writer, so claims can't be duplicated and git operations can't race.
191: 
192: **Back-pressure:**
193: - time budget per tick;
194: - daily budgets for housekeeping calls and tokens;
195: - a circuit breaker after N consecutive failures (like the bug-fixer tick);
196: - a cap on open report conversations.
197: 
198: ### 4.4 Executors and session visibility
199: 
200: | Class | Surface | Executor | Used for |
201: |---|---|---|---|
202: | **Repo work** | IDE | Human sessions, PA workers, the bug-fixer loop | The memory system never changes the repository's code. It *proposes* such work in reports (e.g. "turn invariant X into a CI check", "guide Y contradicts verified claim Z"), for the human or the bug-fixer loop to act on. |
203: | **Reports** | IDE | Antigravity: `agentapi new-conversation`, title prefix `[repo-memory]`, started by the tick. **[R2]** Claude Code: a Desktop local scheduled task (visible under **Scheduled**). | Weekly memory review (claims awaiting approval, gap questions, coverage and health, proposed work); one-off notices such as "OTA backfill ready for review". Only started when there is something to review. |
204: | **Housekeeping** | Headless | `agy -p` with `--model`, `--json-schema`, `--output-format json`, `--input-format stream-json` (stdin, for large payloads and the Windows command-line limit), `--print-timeout`. **[R2]** On Claude Code-only machines: `claude -p --safe-mode --tools "" --system-prompt-file … --json-schema … --no-session-persistence` (§12.2). | All LLM pipeline stages; synthesis for pull tools |
205: | **Mechanical** | No session | The `repo-memory` Go binary in the tick and hooks (§18) | Capture, compaction, entity extraction, index, publishing through a dedicated git worktree |
206: 
207: Everything runs on the user's subscriptions, with no API key and no pay-as-you-go billing:
208: 
209: - **Executor setting.** `housekeeping.executor` is set per machine. In Release 1 it is always `agy`. **[R2]** `claude` becomes available for Claude Code-only machines (decision D2, §17).
210: - **Optional `api` backend.** It exists for other deployments and is off by default.
211: 
212: **Cost of a housekeeping run** (measured 2026-09-30, `gemini-3.8-flash-low`, trivial prompt, empty working directory):
213: 
214: | | |
215: |---|---|
216: | Time | 12.8 s end to end (~5 s model) |
217: | Input tokens | 16,813, almost all fixed agent overhead |
218: | Output tokens | 5 |
219: | Where recorded | Only in the CLI store (`~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/`, project `default-cli-project`); not in the IDE history |
220: 
221: #### 4.4.1 Cost model
222: 
223: Housekeeping cost has two parts: a **fixed overhead per call** (~17k input tokens and ~13 s for `agy -p`) and the **payload**.
224: 
225: **Measured inputs:**
226: 
227: | Transcripts | Count | Median | Mean | Tool traffic |
228: |---|---|---|---|---|
229: | Antigravity top-level, esp32 | 45 surviving | 52k tokens | 120k tokens | 86% |
230: | Antigravity subagent, esp32 | 138 surviving | 29k tokens | 36k tokens | 90% |
231: | Claude Code, esp32 | 35 | ~47k tokens | ~98k tokens | 70% |
232: 
233: Session rates since May: ~1.4 top-level and ~7 subagent Antigravity sessions a day, and ~0.9 Claude Code sessions a day.
234: 
235: The Antigravity sizes above were measured on `transcript.jsonl`, which truncates large fields (§6.2). Untruncated sizes are larger, so the estimates below are lower bounds until P0 re-measures them from `transcript_full.jsonl`.
236:

261: **Isolating housekeeping runs:**
262: - They run with the working directory `<data-dir>/runs/<repo-id>/`, not the repository, so workspace rules and hooks don't load. They use a dedicated `--project` (E7).

289: ### 4.6 Repository enrolment and the kill switch
290: 
291: The plugin is installed globally, so its hooks fire in every workspace the harness opens, and `PreInvocation` fires on every model call. Memory must therefore act only on repositories the user has explicitly enrolled, and must cost almost nothing everywhere else.
292: 
293: **Enrolling a repository.** `repo-memory init`, run in the repository root:
294: 
295: 1. creates `.memory/` (`config.yaml`, `claims/`, `events/`, `views/`) and `.memory/.gitignore` for `.cache/`;
296: 2. adds the map include line to the harness's own instruction file (`GEMINI.md` in Release 1; **[R2]** `CLAUDE.md`), never to the shared `AGENTS.md` (§12.2);
297: 3. registers the repository in `<data-dir>/registry.json`: repo ID, root path and known worktree paths. The repo ID is `sha256(root commit + ":" + canonical origin URL)`, or `sha256(root commit + ":" + real path of the main worktree)` when there is no remote. The root commit alone isn't enough: repositories created from a template such as esp32-app-foundation share their root commit. The ID lives in the machine registry, never in the repository, so a template's committed files can't carry it into a downstream project;
298: 4. offers the subsystem bootstrap (§5.2), whose proposal the user reviews.

1286: ### 12.3 Tick
1287: 
1288: `repo-memory tick` is a subcommand of the `repo-memory` Go binary (§18). It is not a daemon: each run does its work and exits. The order of work, the job table and the budgets are defined in §4.3.
1289: 
1290: - **Idle cost.** A tick with nothing to do makes no LLM calls and finishes in well under a second (program start-up plus a few file and hash checks).
1291: - **Git events** are detected by comparing HEAD, `dependencies.lock` and the sdkconfig hashes with the previous tick. No git hooks are installed.
1292: - **Housekeeping runs** are child processes started with `REPO_MEMORY_HOUSEKEEPING=1`, the working directory `<data-dir>/runs/<repo-id>/`, the configured model and `--print-timeout`. The tick waits for them within its budget; a run still going when the budget ends keeps the tick alive until its timeout, and the next tick skips (`tick.lock`).
1293: - **Reports** are started with `agentapi new-conversation --title="[repo-memory] …"` and polled on later ticks, as in the bug-fixer tick dispatcher.
1294: - **Publishing** runs git in a dedicated worktree (`<data-dir>/<repo-id>/worktrees/<clone-id>/`, branch `memory/pending`), never in the user's checkout. Each clone of the same repository gets its own publishing worktree.

1296: **`repo-memory run`** is kept as an alias for `tick`, for manual use.

1: # WO1 → Architect: Injection Persistence & Token Cost Concern
2: 
3: ## Context
4: E1 proved that `ephemeralMessage` is **per-invocation transient** — visible to the model only during the single invocation where it's injected, then dropped. This has a direct cost implication for the SPEC's §7.2 injection strategy.
5: 
6: ## The Problem
7: The SPEC currently routes **all** context injection through `PreInvocation` → `ephemeralMessage`:
8: - Task brief (1–4k tokens) at `invocationNum == 0`
9: - Touch & error alerts (every invocation)
10: - Déjà-vu tier-1 warnings (every invocation)
11: 
12: Because `invocationNum` resets to 0 on every user prompt, **and** because `ephemeralMessage` doesn't persist across invocations within a prompt cycle, the task brief must be re-injected on every `PreInvocation` call — not just once per prompt.
13: 
14: A typical tool-calling prompt generates 2–10+ invocations. At 2k tokens per injection, that's **4–20k+ wasted tokens per user prompt** on content the model has already seen but can't retain.
15: 
16: ## What We Know (from E1)
17: 
18: | Injection type | Persistence | Tested? |
19: |:---|:---|:---|
20: | `ephemeralMessage` | Per-invocation only (dropped after each invocation) | ✅ Proven (E1, conversations `e9b80453`, `e00ea91f`) |
21: | `userMessage` | **Unknown** — may persist across invocations | ❌ Not tested |
22: | `toolCall` | **Unknown** — may persist across invocations | ❌ Not tested |
23: | System prompt include (`@[...]()` in GEMINI.md) | Persistent, cached | ✅ Known working (MAP.md) |
24: | MCP tool call (model pulls via `memory.brief`) | N/A (pull model, no injection) | ✅ Known working |
25: 
26: ## Proposed Injection Architecture (if `userMessage` persists)
27: 
28: | Content | Mechanism | When | Token cost |
29: |:---|:---|:---|:---|
30: | System map (~2k) | `@[memory map]` include in GEMINI.md | Always-on, cached | **0 marginal** |
31: | Task brief (1–4k) | `userMessage` via `injectSteps` | `invocationNum == 0` only | **Once per prompt** |
32: | Touch/error/déjà-vu alerts (<200 tokens) | `ephemeralMessage` via `injectSteps` | When something is due | **Tiny, acceptable** |
33: | Deep context (on demand) | MCP `memory.brief` / `memory.ask` | Model pulls when needed | **0 injection cost** |
34: 
35: ## Proposed Injection Architecture (if `userMessage` also ephemeral)
36: 
37: | Content | Mechanism | When | Token cost |
38: |:---|:---|:---|:---|
39: | System map (~2k) | `@[memory map]` include in GEMINI.md | Always-on, cached | **0 marginal** |
40: | Task brief (1–4k) | **MCP pull only** (`memory.brief`) | Model decides | **0 injection cost** |
41: | Touch/error/déjà-vu alerts (<200 tokens) | `ephemeralMessage` via `injectSteps` | When something is due | **Tiny, acceptable** |
42: 
43: In this fallback design, `ephemeralMessage` is reserved for sub-200-token nudges — never for bulk context.
44: 
45: ## Required Follow-Up: Experiment E1b
46: 
47: **Test `userMessage` persistence across invocations.** Same methodology as E1:
48: 1. Inject `{"injectSteps": [{"userMessage": "MARKER-USRMSG-4P8W"}]}` at `invocationNum=0`
49: 2. Return `{}` at `invocationNum=1+`
50: 3. At invocation N+5, ask the model if it can see the marker
51: 4. If visible → `userMessage` persists → use it for task brief
52: 5. If not visible → pull-only architecture, no bulk injection
53: 
54: ## Recommendation
55: - **Do not build** the §7.2 injection pipeline assuming `ephemeralMessage` can carry the task brief. The token cost is unacceptable.
56: - **Run E1b first** (one quick test, ~10 minutes) to determine whether `userMessage` is the right vehicle.
57: - **Regardless of E1b outcome**, cap `ephemeralMessage` payloads at ~200 tokens in the SPEC. Bulk context should go via persistent injection or pull.
58: - Consider asking the Antigravity team directly: *"Is `userMessage` in `injectSteps` persistent across invocations within the same prompt cycle, or is it ephemeral like `ephemeralMessage`?"*

1: # E01: `ephemeralMessage` Persistence
2: 
3: ## Question
4: 1. Does an `ephemeralMessage` returned by a PreInvocation hook get delivered to the model?
5: 2. Does it persist in the model's context on later turns?
6: 3. Does it appear in `transcript.jsonl` / `transcript_full.jsonl`?
7: 
8: ## Method
9: 
10: ### Test 1: Wrong Format (Negative Control)
11: 1. Created a hook script (`testdata/e1-marker-hook.sh`) that returned `{"ephemeral_message": "MARKER-ALPHA-7X2Q ..."}` at the top level (snake_case, no `injectSteps` wrapper).
12: 2. Installed as the PreInvocation hook and opened a new conversation (`6a41a111`).
13: 3. Had 6 exchanges (5 with tool calls, 1 asking about the marker).
14: 4. Inspected the transcript for marker presence.
15: 
16: **Result**: Model said **"No, I have not seen either string"**. The markers did NOT appear as `EPHEMERAL_MESSAGE` steps in the transcript. Antigravity silently ignored the malformed hook response.
17: 
18: ### Test 2: Correct Format (Positive Control)
19: 1. Discovered the correct format from Antigravity's hook documentation (`~/.gemini/antigravity/builtin/skills/agy-customizations/docs/hooks.md`):
20:    ```json
21:    {"injectSteps": [{"ephemeralMessage": "..."}]}
22:    ```
23: 2. Updated the hook script to use the correct format: `injectSteps` array with `ephemeralMessage` objects (camelCase).
24: 3. Continued the experiment in conversation `e9b80453` (this session), where the corrected hook was active.
25: 4. Observed the transcript for `EPHEMERAL_MESSAGE` type steps.
26: 
27: **Result**: Markers appeared immediately. Model confirmed seeing `MARKER-ALPHA-7X2Q` in its context.
28: 
29: ### Test 3: Independent Conversation (Definitive)
30: 1. Opened a fresh conversation (`e00ea91f`) with the corrected hook active.
31: 2. Ran 6 prompts requesting tool-calling work, then asked the recall question.
32: 3. Ran 5 more prompts, then asked the recall question a second time.
33: 4. ALPHA was injected at `invocationNum=0` on every user prompt (steps 1, 17, 20).
34: 5. BETA was injected at `invocationNum=1` after tool calls returned (steps 4, 23).
35: 
36: **Recall Test #1 (step 18)**:
37: > - **MARKER-ALPHA-7X2Q**: **Yes, I can see it.** It appears in a `[REPO-MEMORY CONTEXT]` block.
38: > - **MARKER-BETA-9K4R**: **No.** This string does not appear anywhere in my current context.
39: 
40: **Recall Test #2 (step 36, after 5 more exchanges)**:
41: > - **MARKER-ALPHA-7X2Q**: **Yes.** Present in the repo-memory context block.
42: > - **MARKER-BETA-9K4R**: **No.** Not present anywhere in my visible context.
43: 
44: **Critical finding**: BETA was recorded in the transcript at steps 4 and 23 (as `EPHEMERAL_MESSAGE` type), but the model **never saw it**. This proves `ephemeralMessage` is **truly ephemeral per-invocation** — it is injected into the model's context for that specific invocation only and is NOT carried forward to subsequent invocations within the same prompt cycle.
45: 
46: > **Methodology note**: The test conversation initially received all prompts in a single message, then was re-run with individual prompts. This variation actually strengthened the data by exercising multiple invocation patterns across different prompt structures. The core finding (ALPHA visible, BETA invisible) was consistent across all exchanges.
47: 
48: ### Transcript Inspection

93: 2a444abc|Request To Say Hello|default-cli-project
94: ```

103: ## Answer
104: 
105: 1. **`--project` does NOT create a separate namespace.** The flag is silently ignored — all CLI conversations are stored with `project_id = "default-cli-project"` regardless of the `--project` value provided.
106: 
107: 2. **`--continue` does NOT resume housekeeping conversations.** It resumes the most recent conversation in the workspace, which is determined by recency across ALL `default-cli-project` conversations, not by `--project` tag.
108: 
109: 3. **CLI and IDE have fully separate databases.** CLI conversations go to `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/conversation_summaries.db`, IDE conversations to `~/.gemini/antigravity/conversation_summaries.db`. No cross-contamination.
110: 
111: 4. **CLI conversations do NOT appear in the IDE UI.** The housekeeping conversation is invisible to the IDE user.
112: 
113: 5. **Conversations CAN be resumed by explicit ID.** Using `--conversation <id>` can resume any CLI conversation, including housekeeping ones. This means isolation depends on not knowing the conversation ID, not on true namespace separation.
114: 
115: ### Isolation Assessment
116: 
117: | Isolation Vector | Isolated? | Mechanism |
118: |---|---|---|
119: | IDE ↔ CLI stores | ✅ Yes | Separate databases and brain directories |
120: | CLI ↔ CLI conversations | ❌ No | All share `default-cli-project` |
121: | `--project` namespace | ❌ No | Flag is silently ignored |
122: | `--continue` crossover | ⚠️ Partial | Resumes most recent, but could accidentally resume a housekeeping conversation if it was the last one run |
123: | Explicit ID resume | ❌ No | Any conversation can be resumed by ID |
124: 
125: ## SPEC Impact
126: 
127: - **SPEC §Housekeeping**: The `--project` flag cannot be used for isolation. Housekeeping calls are mixed with user CLI conversations in `default-cli-project`. Need an alternative isolation strategy.
128: - **Design decision needed**: Options for housekeeping isolation:
129:   1. Use a non-obvious conversation ID pattern and rely on `--continue` not picking it up (fragile)
130:   2. Use a dedicated agent name (via `--agent`) to tag housekeeping conversations
131:   3. Accept that CLI-level isolation is sufficient (housekeeping won't appear in IDE)
132:   4. File a feature request for proper `--project` namespace support
133: - **SPEC §Cost**: The housekeeping call consumed 16,814 input tokens for a trivial prompt. This is the fixed system prompt overhead. If housekeeping runs every 5 minutes, that's ~4.8M tokens/day just for system prompt overhead.
134: - **Bug/Gap found**: `--project` flag is silently ignored for CLI conversations. Should either work or produce a warning.

104: ## Answer
105: 
106: 1. **Subagents DO fire their own hooks: YES.** Every lifecycle hook (`PreInvocation`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`) fires independently for the subagent. The hooks defined in `.agents/hooks.json` apply to both parent and child conversations.
107: 
108: 2. **Subagent has its own identity: YES.**
109:    - Own `conversationId` (`c33c50f4`, distinct from parent `a955bb7f`)
110:    - Own `transcriptPath` (`.../brain/c33c50f4/.../transcript_full.jsonl`)
111:    - Hook payloads carry the subagent's identity, not the parent's
112: 
113: 3. **Workers are NOT limited to parent sweep — hooks work directly.** The memory plugin can intercept subagent tool calls via `PreToolUse`, inject context via `PreInvocation`, and observe completion via `Stop` — all with the subagent's own conversation context.
114: 
115: ### Critical Additional Findings
116: 
117: - **`PreToolUse` contract is strict**: returning `{}` (no `decision` field) is treated as an implicit deny. The hook MUST return `{"decision": "allow"}` to permit tool execution. This caused a false start where `invoke_subagent` was blocked 3 times.
118: 
119: - **Hook catches `send_message`**: The subagent's `send_message` tool call (used to report back to the parent) also fires `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse`. A hook could intercept or deny inter-agent communication.
120: 
121: - **Hook catches `invoke_subagent`**: The parent's `invoke_subagent` call fires `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse`. A hook could deny subagent spawning.
122: 
123: - **Lifecycle timeline**: The parent's `Stop` hook fires while the subagent is still working (parent goes idle at 21:28:11, subagent starts `run_command` at 21:28:13). The parent is woken by the subagent's `send_message` at 21:28:19.
124: 
125: - **Multiple `PreInvocation` calls**: The subagent fires `PreInvocation` 4 times during its lifecycle (initial, post-tool, post-send, final). Each represents a model invocation within the subagent's prompt cycle.
126: 
127: - **Empty `{}` for PreToolUse = deny**: This silent-failure pattern matches E01 (wrong hook format ignored) and E04 (wrong frontmatter key ignored). Antigravity consistently treats malformed/missing responses as restrictive defaults.
128: 
129: ## SPEC Impact
130: 
131: | SPEC Section | Status | Notes |
132: |:---|:---|:---|
133: | Subagent hook coverage | **Full coverage confirmed** | All 4 hook types fire for subagents |
134: | Subagent identity | **Unique per subagent** | Own `conversationId` and `transcriptPath` |
135: | Hook-based context injection | **Viable for subagents** | `PreInvocation` fires for subagents — can inject task brief |
136: | Hook-based tool gating | **Viable for subagents** | `PreToolUse` fires — can deny/rewrite subagent tool calls |

1: # E09: `deny` + `reason` Behavior
2: 
3: ## Question
4: 1. When a `PreToolUse` hook returns `{"decision": "deny", "reason": "..."}`, does the model see the denial and reason?
5: 2. Does the model re-issue the same call, try a different approach, or abandon?
6: 3. What effect does the **wording** of the reason have on model behavior?
7: 4. In a **batch of parallel tool calls**, does denying one disrupt the others?
8: 5. Does the `overwrite` decision work as a non-blocking advisory?
9: 6. What happens when a hook **command fails** (exits non-zero)?
10: 
11: ## Method
12: 
13: ### Test 1: Basic Deny with Re-Issue Encouragement
14: 1. Created a `PreToolUse` hook script (`testdata/e9-deny-hook.sh`) that returns:
15:    ```json
16:    {"decision": "deny", "reason": "This action was previously tried and failed because the flash partition was misaligned (clm-test-001). If your approach differs, re-issue the call."}
17:    ```
18: 2. Installed via `.agents/hooks.json` with `"matcher": "run_command"`.
19: 3. Opened session `1d574b9a-a225-45bd-a1d9-5f63b94f8b5f`.
20: 4. Asked: *"Run `ls -la` in the current directory"*
21: 
22: **Result**: The model saw the denial and reason. It re-issued 3 times with different approaches:
23: - Attempt 1: `ls -la` → denied
24: - Attempt 2: `/bin/ls -la` (absolute path — model interpreted "different approach" literally) → denied
25: - Attempt 3: `command ls -la` (shell builtin prefix) → denied
26: - Gave up after 3 attempts, concluded "bug or misconfiguration" and offered to help fix the hook.
27: 
28: ### Test 2: Parallel Tool Calls (Selective Deny)
29: 1. Modified the hook to selectively deny: only denies `write_to_file` calls where the target filename contains "denied"; allows all others.
30: 2. Installed via `.agents/hooks.json` with `"matcher": "write_to_file"`.
31: 3. Opened session `f5378730-9894-482e-8f25-b15319efde35`.
32: 4. Asked: *"Create 3 files at once: `/tmp/e9-allowed-one.txt`, `/tmp/e9-denied-two.txt`, `/tmp/e9-allowed-three.txt`"*
33: 
34: **Result**: The model issued 3 parallel `write_to_file` calls (step 1). Results:
35: - Step 2: `e9-allowed-one.txt` → ✅ Created (allowed)
36: - Step 3: `e9-denied-two.txt` → ❌ Denied (hook returned deny)
37: - Step 4: `e9-allowed-three.txt` → ✅ Created (allowed)
38: 
39: The model produced a clean summary table (2 successes, 1 failure) and offered to retry the denied file. **Denial of one call did NOT disrupt the others.**
40: 
41: ### Test 3: Policy-Sounding Wording
42: 1. Changed the deny reason to: *"This action is not permitted because it violates the repository safety policy. File writes to the /tmp directory are restricted during testing."*
43: 2. Opened session `579ab124-8d36-4124-988c-b1e97afd2853`.
44: 3. Asked: *"Run `ls -la` in the current directory"*
45: 
46: **Result**: The model retried twice (fewer than the 3 retries with "re-issue if different"):
47: - Attempt 1: `ls -la` → denied
48: - Attempt 2: `ls -la /full/path` → denied
49: - Pivoted to `view_file` (a completely different tool) instead of retrying `run_command`.
50: 
51: ### Test 4: `overwrite` Decision
52: 1. Changed the hook to return:
53:    ```json
54:    {"decision": "allow", "reason": "Command modified for safety.", "overwrite": {"CommandLine": "echo 'HOOK-REWRITTEN: The original command was intercepted.'"}}
55:    ```
56: 2. Observed in the **live experiment session** (`41ec4be3`) when hooks.json was hot-reloaded.
57: 
58: **Result**: The overwrite worked:
59: - The original command did NOT execute.
60: - The rewritten command (`echo 'HOOK-REWRITTEN...'`) executed instead.
61: - The tool output was prefixed with: *"A pre-tool hook changed the arguments of this tool call before it ran. Changed: CommandLine."*
62: - The model saw both the notice and the rewritten output.
63: 
64: ### Test 5: Hook Command Failure (Exit Non-Zero)
65: 1. First attempt at E9 had a broken hook path (`./testdata/e9-deny-hook.sh` — resolved relative to `.agents/` not repo root).
66: 2. The hook command failed with exit code 127 (`sh: ./testdata/e9-deny-hook.sh: No such file or directory`).
67: 3. Observed in sessions `ab689674` (test session) and `41ec4be3` (experiment session).
68: 
69: **Result**:
70: - **Hook failures BLOCK tool execution** — the tool call does not proceed when the hook command exits non-zero.
71: - The error is delivered to the model as: `"tool call denied by pre-tool hook: ..."` (same format as an explicit deny).
72: - The error includes the stderr output from the failed command.
73: - The model treats a hook failure identically to an explicit deny — it sees the error and tries to work around it.
74: 
75: ### Bonus Finding: hooks.json Hot-Reload
76: - Initially hypothesized that hooks.json was cached at session start.
77: - **Disproven**: hooks.json changes were picked up mid-session. The earlier "caching" behavior was because the script file path was wrong (resolving from `.agents/` directory).
78: - Confirmed: when hooks.json was modified to point to the overwrite hook, the change was picked up by the existing session without restart.
79: 
80: ## Raw Evidence
81: 
82: ### Test 1 — Deny with Re-Issue (session `1d574b9a`, steps 1-7)
83: ```
84: step=1: tool_call: run_command "ls -la"
85: step=2: ERROR: "tool call denied by pre-tool hook: This action was previously tried and
86:         failed because the flash partition was misaligned (clm-test-001). If your approach
87:         differs, re-issue the call."
88: step=3: tool_call: run_command "/bin/ls -la"  [model tried different approach]
89: step=4: ERROR: same deny reason
90: step=5: tool_call: run_command "command ls -la"  [model tried another variant]
91: step=6: ERROR: same deny reason
92: step=7: "All `run_command` calls are being blocked by a pre-tool hook. This looks like
93:         a bug or misconfiguration..."  [gave up]
94: ```
95: 
96: ### Test 2 — Parallel Calls (session `f5378730`, steps 1-5)
97: ```
98: step=1: 3 parallel write_to_file calls:
99:         - /tmp/e9-allowed-one.txt
100:         - /tmp/e9-denied-two.txt
101:         - /tmp/e9-allowed-three.txt
102: step=2: e9-allowed-one.txt → DONE (created)
103: step=3: e9-denied-two.txt → ERROR (denied by hook)
104: step=4: e9-allowed-three.txt → DONE (created)
105: step=5: Model summary: "Two out of three files were created successfully."
106:         | e9-allowed-one.txt   | ✅ Created |
107:         | e9-denied-two.txt    | ❌ Failed  |
108:         | e9-allowed-three.txt | ✅ Created |
109: ```
110: 
111: ### Test 3 — Policy Wording (session `579ab124`, steps 1-7)
112: ```
113: step=1: tool_call: run_command "ls -la"
114: step=2: ERROR: "tool call denied by pre-tool hook: This action is not permitted because
115:         it violates the repository safety policy."
116: step=3: tool_call: run_command "ls -la /full/path"  [retried once]
117: step=4: ERROR: same deny
118: step=5: Pivoted to view_file instead of retrying run_command [gave up on run_command]
119: ```
120: 
121: ### Test 4 — Overwrite (session `41ec4be3`, live)
122: ```
123: Tool output prefix: "A pre-tool hook changed the arguments of this tool call before it
124: ran. Changed: CommandLine."
125: Actual output: "HOOK-REWRITTEN: The original command was intercepted and replaced by
126: the safety hook."
127: ```
128: 
129: ### Test 5 — Hook Failure (session `ab689674`)
130: ```
131: ERROR: "JSON hook "jsonhook__e9-deny-probe_PreToolUse_0_0" failed: command failed:
132: exit status 127, stderr: sh: ./testdata/e9-deny-hook.sh: No such file or directory"
133: ```
134: 
135: ## Answer
136: 
137: 1. **Model sees deny + reason: YES.** The reason string is delivered verbatim in the error message, prefixed with *"tool call denied by pre-tool hook:"*. The model reads and reasons about the content.
138: 
139: 2. **Re-issue vs. abandon depends on wording:**
140:    - *"If your approach differs, re-issue the call"* → model retried **3 times** with different command variants (absolute path, `command` prefix), interpreting "different approach" as command variation.
141:    - *"This action is not permitted"* (policy-sounding) → model retried **2 times**, then pivoted to a completely different tool (`view_file`). Policy language caused faster abandonment.
142:    - In both cases, the model eventually concluded the hook was misconfigured and gave up.
143: 
144: 3. **Parallel call denial is isolated: YES.** Denying one tool call in a parallel batch does NOT prevent the others from executing. Each call is independently evaluated by the hook. The model receives individual success/error results for each call.
145: 
146: 4. **`overwrite` decision works as a non-blocking rewrite:**
147:    - The original arguments are replaced (shallow merge) before execution.
148:    - A notice is prepended to the tool output: *"A pre-tool hook changed the arguments of this tool call before it ran. Changed: [key names]."*
149:    - The model sees both the notice and the rewritten output.
150:    - This is usable as a **non-blocking advisory** — the tool executes but with modified arguments.
151: 
152: 5. **Hook failures = implicit deny:** When the hook command fails (non-zero exit), the tool call is blocked. The error message replaces the tool output. The model treats it identically to an explicit deny.
153: 
154: 6. **hooks.json is hot-reloaded** — changes are picked up mid-session without restart.
155: 
156: ### Wording Impact Summary
157: 
158: | Wording Style | Retries Before Giving Up | Model Behavior |
159: |:---|:---:|:---|
160: | *"Re-issue if your approach differs"* (advisory) | 3 | Tried command variants (absolute path, `command` prefix) |
161: | *"Not permitted... safety policy"* (policy) | 2 | Tried one variant, then pivoted to different tool entirely |
162: 
163: ### Hook Path Resolution
164: - Hook `command` paths in `hooks.json` resolve **relative to the `hooks.json` directory**, NOT the repo root.
165: - For `.agents/hooks.json`, the working directory is `.agents/`.
166: - Use **absolute paths** to avoid ambiguity.
167: 
168: ## SPEC Impact
169: 
170: | SPEC Section | Status | Notes |
171: |:---|:---|:---|
172: | `deny` + `reason` delivery | **Confirmed** | Reason string delivered verbatim to model as error |
173: | Deny behavior | **Model retries then gives up** | Advisory wording → more retries; policy wording → fewer |
174: | Parallel call isolation | **Confirmed** | Each call independently evaluated; denials are isolated |
175: | `overwrite` decision | **Confirmed working** | Non-blocking rewrite with notice; usable for advisory/steering |
176: | Hook failure behavior | **Implicit deny** | Non-zero exit blocks tool execution |
177: | hooks.json reload | **Hot-reloaded mid-session** | Changes picked up without restart |
178: | Hook path resolution | **Relative to hooks.json directory** | `.agents/hooks.json` → cwd is `.agents/` |
179: | Déjà-vu design | **Validated** | `deny` + reason is viable for "this was tried before" warnings; advisory wording triggers retries (good for suggesting alternatives); policy wording causes faster abandonment (good for hard blocks) |
180: | Overwrite for steering | **New capability** | Can rewrite tool args non-destructively; model sees the rewrite notice; usable for command sanitization or injection of safety flags |

1: # E10: Housekeeping Overhead Reduction
2: 
3: > **Experiment ID:** E10
4: > **Date:** 2026-10-01
5: > **Status:** Complete
6: > **Platform:** macOS (Apple Silicon), `agy` CLI v1.2.14
7: 
8: ## Question
9: 
10: What is the fixed token overhead of a housekeeping `agy -p` call, and can it be reduced below the ~17k token baseline?
11: 
12: ## Method
13: 
14: 1. Ran `agy -p --output-format json "Return the word HELLO"` with different configurations
15: 2. Compared `input_tokens` across: default config, minimal agent definition, disabled slash commands, sandbox mode, and non-workspace directory
16: 3. Tested prefix caching by running 5 identical calls in quick succession
17: 4. Compared overhead between Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash model families
18: 
19: ## Raw Evidence
20: 
21: ### Overhead by Configuration
22: 
23: | Configuration | Input Tokens | Delta from Baseline | Notes |
24: |---|---|---|---|
25: | Default config, from repo dir | 16,810 | — | Baseline |
26: | Default config, from /tmp | 16,660 | -150 | No GEMINI.md or workspace-specific rules |
27: | `--agent '{"identity":{"name":"test"}}'` | 16,809 | -1 | Minimal agent definition has no effect |
28: | `--disable-slash-commands` | 16,815 | +5 | Flag itself adds a token or two, no reduction |
29: | `--sandbox` | 17,593 | +783 | Sandbox restrictions added to system prompt |
30: | Gemini 3.6 Flash (Low), from repo | ~9,930 | -6,880 | **Different model family, dramatically lower** |
31: 
32: ### Prefix Caching Test (5 runs, Gemini 3.8 Flash Low)
33: ```
34: run 1: in=16,816 cache_read=0 out=1 dur=6.6s wall=11.8s
35: run 2: in=16,809 cache_read=0 out=1 dur=7.0s wall=13.9s
36: run 3: in=16,816 cache_read=0 out=1 dur=3.4s wall=10.1s
37: run 4: in=16,808 cache_read=0 out=1 dur=4.5s wall=12.1s
38: run 5: in=16,811 cache_read=0 out=1 dur=4.5s wall=11.0s
39: ```
40: **Result: No prefix caching observed.** `cache_read_tokens = 0` for all 5 runs despite identical prompts. Each `agy -p` call creates a new conversation, preventing session-level prefix caching.
41: 
42: ### Model Family Comparison (Gemini 3.6 Flash Low)
43: ```
44: call 1: in=18,073 out=1 dur=5.0s wall=11.1s
45: call 2: in=9,933  out=1 dur=5.1s wall=12.2s
46: call 3: in=9,925  out=1 dur=6.0s wall=10.7s
47: call 4: in=9,929  out=1 dur=4.6s wall=11.6s
48: call 5: in=9,926  out=1 dur=3.8s wall=10.4s
49: ```
50: First call anomalously high (18,073), subsequent calls ~9,930. This suggests either:
51: - Different tokenizer efficiency between model families
52: - First-call system prompt compilation cost amortized across session
53: - Different skill/tool rendering for older model versions
54: 
55: ### Timing Breakdown
56: ```
57: Total wall time per call: 10-14s
58:   - API duration:  3-7s (model inference)
59:   - CLI overhead:  6-7s (process startup, auth, conversation setup)
60: ```
61: 
62: ### Token Budget Breakdown (estimated)
63: 
64: The ~16.8k tokens for Gemini 3.8 Flash comprise:
65: - **System prompt** (identity, communication style, guidelines): ~2-3k tokens
66: - **Tool descriptions** (30+ tools with full JSON schemas): ~6-8k tokens
67: - **Skill descriptions** (25+ skills with trigger descriptions): ~3-4k tokens
68: - **MCP server listings**: ~1-2k tokens
69: - **User rules** (GEMINI.md includes): ~150 tokens
70: - **Workspace/conversation metadata**: ~500 tokens
71: - **User prompt**: ~10 tokens
72: 
73: ## Answer
74: 
75: 1. **The fixed overhead is ~16.8k tokens for Gemini 3.8 Flash, ~9.9k for Gemini 3.6 Flash.** The overhead cannot be reduced below these floors with any available CLI flags.
76: 
77: 2. **No available mechanism to disable plugins per-call.** The `--agent` flag does not suppress plugin/skill loading. The `--disable-slash-commands` flag only affects slash command expansion, not system prompt size. No `--no-plugins` or `--no-skills` flag exists.
78: 
79: 3. **Prefix caching does NOT work for `agy -p` calls.** Each call creates a new conversation with a new conversation ID, which prevents the API from recognizing the system prompt as a cache-hit. This means every housekeeping call pays the full ~17k input token cost.
80: 
81: 4. **Model family choice has a major impact.** Gemini 3.6 Flash uses ~9.9k tokens vs ~16.8k for Gemini 3.8 Flash — a 41% reduction. This is likely due to different tokenizer efficiency and/or a simpler system prompt for older models.
82: 
83: 5. **CLI overhead adds ~6-7 seconds per call.** The wall-clock time includes process startup, auth token acquisition, and conversation setup — significant for high-frequency housekeeping.
84: 
85: ### Cost Projection
86: 
87: At 1 housekeeping call per minute:
88: | Model | Tokens/call | Tokens/day | Tokens/month |
89: |---|---|---|---|
90: | Gemini 3.8 Flash (Low) | 16,810 | 24.2M | 726M |
91: | Gemini 3.6 Flash (Low) | 9,930 | 14.3M | 429M |
92: 
93: At current Gemini Flash pricing (~$0.075/1M input tokens), this is:
94: - Gemini 3.8: ~$1.82/month
95: - Gemini 3.6: ~$1.07/month
96: 
97: The token cost is manageable, but the 10-14s wall-clock time per call makes 1-call-per-minute infeasible via `agy -p`.
98: 
99: ## SPEC Impact
100: 
101: - **SPEC §Housekeeping**: The ~17k token floor is an irreducible cost of the `agy -p` approach. Cannot be reduced with current CLI flags.
102: - **Design decision needed**: Prefix caching requires same-conversation continuation. The housekeeping engine should use `--conversation` to resume a persistent housekeeping conversation rather than creating new conversations each time. This could enable prefix caching and reduce ongoing token costs.
103: - **Design consideration**: Consider Gemini 3.6 Flash for housekeeping tasks — 41% fewer tokens with equivalent capability for simple memory pipeline operations.
104: - **Design consideration**: The 10-14s wall-clock time per `agy -p` call means the housekeeping engine should batch operations within a single conversation turn rather than spawning many short calls.
105: - **Alternative path**: Instead of `agy -p`, consider using the direct API (via MCP or Go SDK) to avoid CLI overhead entirely. A direct API call with a minimal system prompt could reduce to ~500 tokens.

630: 
631: ---
632: 
633: ## 6. Pipeline
634: 
635: ### 6.1 Stage summary
636: 
637: | Stage | Input | Output | Engine | Cost profile |
638: |---|---|---|---|---|
639: | 0 Capture | `Stop` hook (event) or tick sweep (time) | Queue entry plus transcript copy | Script | ~0 |
640: | 1 Compact | Raw transcript | Episode | Deterministic | ~0 LLM |
641: | 2 Triage | Episode | Keep/skip plus reasons | Rules, then small model | Low; most sessions stop here |
642: | 3 Extract | Kept episode | Candidate claims | Small model, batched | Medium, input-heavy |
643: | 4 Reconcile | Candidate plus existing claims on the same anchors | Claim ops | Stronger model, small inputs | Low per candidate |
644: | 5 Verify | Claim ops | Verified ops | Deterministic plus targeted small-model check | Low |
645: | 6 Publish | Verified ops | Claim files, views, memory PR | Deterministic plus view synthesis | Low |
646: 
647: ### 6.2 Stage 0: Capture
648: 
649: Capture uses both invocation paths (§4.1). The event path captures sessions promptly; the time path guarantees that nothing is missed.
650: 
651: **Event path (primary).** The `Stop` hook:
652: 
653: 1. writes `{harness, conversation_id, transcript_path, repo_root, branch, head}` to `spool/`;
654: 2. copies the primary transcript source (`transcript_full.jsonl`, or its chunks when the monolithic file is absent) into `queue/` **incrementally**: only bytes appended since the last copy. The byte offset and a hash of the already-copied prefix are kept in `state/`. If the prefix hash no longer matches (the harness rewrote the file, reportedly when the user branches or edits an earlier step), the file is copied in full once. Without this, a long session would re-copy multi-megabyte transcripts on every turn;
655: 3. returns immediately.
656: 
657: It never returns `"decision": "continue"`. `Stop` fires whenever the execution loop ends, so a conversation with several user turns produces several `Stop` events. Each one re-copies the transcript. Processing waits until the conversation has been idle for 15 minutes (checked by the next tick), so the same conversation isn't extracted repeatedly mid-flight.
658: 
659: **Time path (backstop).** Every tick sweeps the transcript locations for files whose modification time or size changed since the last cursor:
660: 
661: - Antigravity app and IDE: `~/.gemini/antigravity/brain/<conversation-id>/.system_generated/logs/transcript.jsonl` (steps with `step_index`, `source`, `type`, `status`, `created_at`, `content` / `thinking` / `tool_calls`);
662: - Antigravity CLI: the same layout under `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/`. The two stores share most conversation IDs, so sessions are de-duplicated by conversation ID.
663: - **[R2]** Claude Code: `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`, plus subagent transcripts in `<session-id>/subagents/*.jsonl` (PA workers spawned with the `Agent` tool live there).
664:   - Default retention is 30 days (`cleanupPeriodDays`).
665:   - Anthropic documents the entry format as internal and version-dependent, so the Claude Code parser is version-aware and tolerant (§12.2).
666:   - As insurance against parser breaks, the Claude Code `Stop` hook also appends the turn's essentials (prompt, tool names, error excerpts, commit commands), taken from hook inputs, to a harness-neutral side-log in the spool.
667: 
668: **Antigravity transcript file set.** Each conversation's `logs/` directory holds two monolithic files and their chunked copies. Verified across all 537 conversations on the reference machine:
669: 
670: | Source | Content | Use |
671: |---|---|---|
672: | `transcript_full.jsonl` | Complete and untruncated; never contains `truncated_fields`; matches `transcript.jsonl` line for line | **Primary** |
673: | `chunks/transcript_full/*.jsonl` | The same bytes as `transcript_full.jsonl`, sliced at exact 102,400-byte (100 KiB) offsets | **Fallback 1**, if the monolithic file is absent |
674: | `transcript.jsonl` | Large fields truncated and marked `"truncated_fields": ["content", "thinking", "tool_calls"]` (494 of 537 transcripts have such lines) | **Fallback 2**, with truncated steps flagged in the episode |
675: | `chunks/transcript/*.jsonl` | The same bytes as `transcript.jsonl`, sliced the same way | Last resort |
676: 
677: Chunk files are **byte slices, not line-aligned JSONL.** Every non-final chunk is exactly 102,400 bytes, and a record that straddles a boundary is split between two files. Chunks must be concatenated in lexical filename order into one byte stream (`io.MultiReader`) before splitting on newlines. Parsing chunk files individually fails on both halves of every boundary record, and counting their lines separately double-counts boundary records; that is what made an earlier line-count comparison look as if chunks held extra steps.
678: 
679: The parser therefore reads one source, in the order above, and never merges sources. Step-index gaps (§6.2, transcript completeness) are present identically in both monolithic files, so they are recorded as gaps; their cause remains part of E12.
680: 
681: It copies each changed transcript into the queue. Sessions are attributed to a repo via `conversation_summaries.db` `workspace_uris` for Antigravity and the project directory for Claude Code. This covers:
682: 
683: - crashed or killed sessions where `Stop` never fired;
684: - subagent sessions, if they don't fire their own `Stop` hooks (experiment E8);
685: - sessions from before installation (backfill of whatever still survives);
686: - long sessions: a session still in progress is re-copied each tick, and processing waits until it has been idle for 15 minutes.
687: 
688: **Commit linkage.** This happens in the tick, not in hooks. Commits made on the session's branch between session start and end are matched from `git log` and reflog, and confirmed against commit commands in the transcript. No hook records tool outcomes for capture: the transcript already has them. (`PostToolUse` is used only to detect git operations that trigger re-checks, §4.2.)
689: 
690: **Recursion guard.** Housekeeping runs (§4.4) are excluded from capture entirely, identified by their dedicated project and working directory. Report conversations (`[repo-memory]` title prefix) are captured, but only the human's messages in them count as evidence. Other autonomous sessions, such as bug-fixer loop conversations and their trajectory reviews, are captured normally. They are a rich source of failure signatures.
691: 
692: **Transcript completeness.** Antigravity inserts `CHECKPOINT` steps into long transcripts. In a sample of 566 transcripts, 340 had checkpoints and 257 had small gaps in their step indices (at most a few dozen steps out of 1,000+). The sweep records the gaps in the episode header; it doesn't treat them as errors.
693: 
694: Capture never calls an LLM. The `Stop` hook budget is ≤ 200 ms.
695: 
696: ### 6.3 Stage 1: Compact
697: 
698: Apply the compaction rules in §5.1 and scrub secrets. Record `raw_chars` and `kept_chars`. Target a reduction of ≥ 3× (Appendix A.2 suggests ~70% of transcript volume is tool traffic already held by git).
699: 
700: ### 6.4 Stage 2: Triage
701: 
702: **Rules (cheap, first):**
703: 
704: - Keep if any hold:
705:   - a failure outcome followed later by a success on the same target;
706:   - a revert or abandoned edit;
707:   - a user message containing a decision, preference, correction or approval signal (approving an approach is as informative as correcting one);
708:   - a new file under a subsystem glob;
709:   - a dependency or config change;
710:   - reasoning spans above a length threshold discussing alternatives;
711:   - a device or soak outcome;
712:   - a write to a memory artefact, or a `memory.note` call (see below).
713: - Skip if all hold: no failures, no commits, fewer than K steps, and no decision signals.
714: 
715: **Memory-artefact writes.** When a working agent or the PA writes to a memory artefact, that is its own judgement, made with full context at the moment of learning, that something was worth keeping. Detecting it costs nothing, because compaction already sees every edit path. Until P4 retires hand-written PA knowledge (§13), these writes are frequent.
716: 
717: - **Configuration.** The paths are set in `config.yaml` → `triage.memory_artefacts`. The default is the PA workspace's `MEMORY.md`, `PROJECT.md` and `WORKORDER.md` files, plus any harness-native memory store the adapter declares.
718: - **Leads, not evidence.** The written text is kept as `note` steps (§5.1). It points extraction at the right steps, and P13 applies to it as to any agent text.
719: 
720: A **small model** handles the ambiguous remainder, answering "Is there durable, repo-specific knowledge here?" with reasons. Up to 20 episode synopses go into one call.
721: 
722: **Salience windows (mechanical, no LLM).** For each kept episode, triage also selects the step ranges that extraction will read:
723: 
724: | Window around | Extent |
725: |---|---|
726: | A failure and its eventual fix or abandonment | From the first failure to 2 steps after the success or abandonment |
727: | A revert or abandoned edit | ±5 steps |
728: | A human message with a decision, preference, correction or approval signal | ±3 steps; human messages themselves are always included |
729: | A write to a memory artefact | The `note` step, plus the steps back to the start of the failure, discussion or decision it records (at most 20) |
730: | A reasoning span that weighs alternatives, or a human message that sets a constraint or trade-off | The span, +2 steps. Detected lexically in `thinking`, agent text and human messages, using a configurable marker list (default: "trade-off", "instead of", "rather than", "decided to", "because", "invariant", "constraint", "must not", "do not use", "ADR"). Capped at 2 such windows per episode, so smooth "green-path" design decisions that never fail a build still reach extraction without eroding compaction. |
731: | A device, flash or soak outcome | ±5 steps |
732: 
733: Each episode also gets a **synopsis**: files touched grouped by subsystem, commits, the outcome list, exposures, and every human message verbatim. Windows plus synopsis should roughly halve the extraction payload (§4.4.1). Recall is the risk. B5 lists durable knowledge the extractor missed, and if misses fall outside windows, the window rules widen.
734: 
735: ### 6.5 Stage 3: Extract
736: 
737: **Input:** the episode's synopsis and salience windows (§6.4), plus the entity list for the subsystems it touched (names only). Episodes are packed into one call up to the 60k payload cap, with a parent session and its subagents first.
738: 
739: **Output:**
740: - candidate claims, each with type, statement, `relevant_when` and `apply` lines (§5.3), anchors (by entity reference), conditions, `closes_when` for `open-issue` candidates (§5.3.1), evidence (step indices and outcomes), proposed status and extraction rationale;
741: - `gaps`: things the episode relied on that match neither a claim nor an entity, such as an external service, a protocol detail or a board quirk. They feed coverage (§9.1).
742: 
743: Extraction rules, enforced by prompt and schema:
744: 
745: 1. **Store only what the code can't tell you.** Reject claims that restate code structure.
746: 2. **Status from outcomes.** `observed` or better requires a tool outcome at the cited step. Otherwise the claim is a `hypothesis`.
747: 3. **Failure triage** (from Dream-RSI's policy prompt). Each failed attempt is classified as `approach-unrecoverable`, `implementation-bug`, `environment` or `insufficient-evidence`. Only `approach-unrecoverable` yields a `ruled-out` claim. Implementation bugs yield at most a `failure-signature`.
748: 4. **Human statements** become candidates with `evidence.kind: human`. Reconcile promotes them to `confirmed` if they're decisions.
749: 5. **Conditions** are captured whenever a claim depends on a version, board, chip or config value.
750: 6. **External content** (web pages, issue text, third-party docs quoted in the session) is tagged `provenance: external` (§11.2).
751: 7. **Evidence independence (P13).** Cited evidence may only be tool outcomes (not from memory tools) and `human`-authored steps. Agent text and reasoning are where candidates come from, never what supports them. Automation-authored steps are never evidence.
752: 8. **Exposure awareness.** The extractor sees the episode's exposure steps. A candidate that restates a claim the session was exposed to earlier is marked `echo_of: clm-…` rather than presented as new knowledge.
753: 9. **Match blocks for ruled-out claims.** Every `ruled-out` candidate carries a `match` block: the concrete commands, config keys, symbols and parameter values from the failed attempts. Stage 5 checks that each term actually appears in those attempts, so déjà-vu tier 1 (§7.6) has precise terms to match.
754: 10. **Notes are leads.** A `note` step (§5.1) shows what an agent thought was durable. A candidate drawn from it still needs a tool outcome or a human step as evidence (rule 7), and it is restated from the evidence rather than copied from the note.
755: 11. **Work status is referenced, not restated.** Where the PA ledger, an issue or a branch already records the state of some work, an `open-issue` claim points at it through `closes_when` instead of copying the state into its text.
756: 
757: ### 6.6 Stage 4: Reconcile
758: 
759: For each candidate:
760: 
761: 1. Look up existing claims sharing any anchor, plus claims on the same subsystem of the same type (deterministic, bounded to 30 or fewer).
762: 2. The stronger model decides one operation:
763: 
764: | Op | Effect |
765: |---|---|
766: | `create` | New claim |
767: | `support` | Add evidence to an existing claim; may raise status (e.g. `observed` → `verified` on second independent episode) |
768: | `refine` | Edit the statement or conditions of an existing claim (keeps ID; old text kept in history) |
769: | `contradict` | Record `contradicts`; if the new evidence is stronger by the trust ladder, mark the old claim `refuted` |
770: | `supersede` | New claim replaces the old one (design changed); old one becomes `superseded` |
771: | `promote` | e.g. `hypothesis` → `verified` when this episode tested it successfully |
772: | `discard` | Duplicate or not durable |
773: 
774: 3. Ops that would lower the status of a `confirmed` claim are never applied automatically. They're queued for human review.
775: 4. **Evidence independence (P13).** When the episode was exposed to the claim before the candidate's evidence:
776: 
777: | Situation after exposure | Treatment |
778: |---|---|
779: | The agent restates or follows the claim; outcomes are consistent but don't test it (e.g. followed an invariant and the build passed) | No `support`. The exposure is recorded as `used` for push-precision metrics only (§10.1). |
780: | A new outcome **tests** the claim, i.e. it would have come out differently had the claim been false (e.g. a ruled-out approach retried and failed the same way; a failure signature matched and its fix resolved the error) | `support` is allowed, with the outcome as evidence, **only if a mechanical precondition holds first:** after the exposure step, the session edited, built, tested or ran something touching at least one of the claim's anchored files or symbols, or ran the claim's `enforced_by` check. An unrelated green build after reading the map never qualifies. The reconciler's judgement that the outcome tests the claim is applied only to candidates that pass the precondition. |
781: | An outcome contradicts the claim | `contradict`, handled normally and flagged as high-value: memory was followed and was wrong |
782: | A human explicitly confirms or corrects the claim | Counts as human evidence (`confirmed` or a correction). A human message that merely continues the work ("ok, carry on") doesn't. |
783: 
784: This applies to every session, including bug-fixer conversations and report conversations. The count of suppressed supports is reported (§10.1).
785: 
786: ### 6.7 Stage 5: Verify
787: 
788: - **Anchor resolution:** every anchor must resolve on the claim's scope branch. Compute fingerprints (symbol body hash, config value, file-window hash).
789: - **Behavioural check:** for `invariant`, `fact` and `decision` claims about code behaviour, a small model reads *only* the anchored snippets and answers "Is this statement consistent with this code?" Inconsistent claims get the `needs-review` flag.
790: - **Branch scoping:**
791: 
792: | Event | Effect |
793: |---|---|
794: | Claim from a branch not yet merged | `scope.branch = <branch>`; delivered only in sessions on that branch or its descendants |
795: | Branch merged to main | Scope moves to `main`; `merged` status is available |
796: | Branch abandoned (deleted unmerged, marked abandoned by the PA, or idle > 30 days unmerged) | `ruled-out` and `failure-signature` claims are promoted to `main` scope; others are retired with a note |
797: | Commit reverted on main | Claims whose evidence was that commit are re-evaluated; the revert is itself evidence |
798: 
799: ### 6.8 Stage 6: Publish
800: 
801: - Write or update claim files and regenerate the affected views.
802: - Measure each synthesised view against its budget (§5.5). An over-budget view is re-synthesised once, with the overshoot stated and an instruction to shorten, rather than truncated. If it is still over, its lowest-priority sections are replaced by links to the claim index.
803: 
804: Publishing has two lanes, so review never delays value (P12).
805: 
806: **Local lane (immediate).** New and changed claims are written to `<data-dir>/<repo-id>/pending/` and indexed straight away. On this machine, delivery uses them at their evidence status, marked `unreviewed`. Exceptions: security-sensitive claims (§11.2) and `provenance: external` claims are never delivered until reviewed.
807: 
808: **Shared lane (reviewed).**
809: 
810: - Pending ops are batched into a **memory PR** on branch `memory/pending`, opened or updated daily by default. Nothing is ever committed to the user's current branch or directly to main.
811: - The PR description groups ops by subsystem with evidence links. It highlights anything touching `confirmed` claims, `invariant` claims or security-relevant subsystems.
812: - Once merged, claims leave `pending/` and are read from `.memory/claims/`.
813: 
814: **Review profiles** (`config.yaml` → `review.profile`):
815: 
816: | Op | `solo` (default) | `team` |
817: |---|---|---|
818: | `support`, `promote` on non-security claims | Auto-merged | Auto-merged |
819: | `create`, `refine` of `fact`, `failure-signature`, `procedure`, `convention` | Auto-merged at `verified` or higher; listed in a weekly digest | Reviewed |
820: | `create`, `refine` of `invariant`, `decision`, `ruled-out` | Reviewed | Reviewed |
821: | Anything that lowers a `confirmed` claim, touches security-relevant subsystems, or has `provenance: external` | Reviewed | Reviewed |
822: 
823: Auto-merged ops are still visible in the PR history, and any of them can be reverted.
824: 
825: ### 6.9 Model and cost policy
826: 
827: - **Small model** for triage, extract and behavioural verify. **Stronger model** for reconcile and view synthesis only.
828: - **Executor:** housekeeping runs via `agy -p` on the user's Antigravity quota, or (**[R2]**) via `claude -p --safe-mode` on Claude Code-only machines (§4.4, D2). No API key and no batch API. The cost model is in §4.4.1.
829: - **Model per stage**, chosen in `config.yaml` from `agy models`. Defaults:
830:   - `gemini-3.8-flash-low` for triage and verify;
831:   - `gemini-3.8-flash-medium` for extraction;
832:   - `gemini-3.1-pro-low` for reconcile and view synthesis.
833: - **Every LLM stage is a pure function:** deterministic context assembly, one `agy -p` call with `--json-schema`, then the result is written. No tool use inside housekeeping runs. That makes stages batchable, retryable, idempotent and replayable during re-projection.
834: - **Optional `api` backend.** A direct-API executor (with provider batch APIs and caching) is part of the design for other deployments. It is off by default and unused here.
835: - Hard caps per episode: extraction input ≤ 60k tokens (split larger episodes by subagent or phase); ≤ 20 candidates per episode.
836: - Daily budgets for housekeeping calls and tokens (from the `agy` usage output). The backfill is throttled by them: OTA and BLE first, then the rest by churn.
837: - The tick records token spend per stage and per housekeeping run (§10.4).

869: ### 7.2 Task start
870: 
871: 1. Always-on: `MAP.md`, loaded by the harness's own instruction file. 872: 2. At the first model invocation, the delivery hook reads the task text (first user message) and branch from the transcript.
873: 3. The hook links the task to entities using the local index:
874:    - lexical match on entity names, paths, symbols and error strings;
875:    - plus files already open or mentioned;
876:    - if lexical matching yields nothing, the hook injects the map-level summary with a one-line pointer to the claim indexes (§5.5), so the agent can choose the relevant subsystems itself at once. If it needs the brief sooner, the agent can call `memory.brief` synchronously (~13 s). An LLM is never called inside a hook.

878:    1. invariants of the involved subsystems;
879:    2. open issues and in-flight work;
880:    3. ruled-out approaches;
881:    4. relevant procedures;
882:    5. decisions.

925: 
926: The main defence against repeating a dead-end is not an alert at all:
927: 
928: - **Tier 0: proactive delivery (primary).** Ruled-out approaches for an entity are delivered in the task brief (§7.2) and on first touch of that entity (§7.3), before any plan to retry exists. Most prevention happens here.
929: - **Tier 1: lexical safety net.** It catches a concrete retry as it is proposed.
930: - **Tier 2: late correction.** On Antigravity it arrives about a minute behind, so it corrects the *next* attempt rather than preventing the first. On Claude Code it arrives in seconds through `asyncRewake` (§12.2).
931: 
932: **Tier 1: lexical (no LLM).**
933: 
934: - Every `ruled-out` claim carries a `match` block, generated at extraction from the failed attempts' concrete commands, config keys, symbols and values (§6.5, rule 9). Example: `any: ["vTaskDelay", "INT_WDT_TIMEOUT", "CHECK_CPU1"]` scoped to the entities `BLEStack::init` and `NimBLEDevice::init`.
935: - A match requires two conditions:
936:   1. an anchored entity is in play in the session (touched or mentioned);
937:   2. the claim's `match` terms appear in the text being checked.
938: - **At `PreToolUse`**, the hook checks the concrete proposed command or edit, and also the current turn's reasoning at the transcript tail (the `thinking` that produced this call), if E3 shows the transcript is current at that point. A match against a `verified` or stronger `ruled-out` claim uses `gate-once`: `deny` with "This was tried on <date> and failed because <reason> (clm-…). If your approach differs, re-issue the call." This is the only way to catch the retry *before* it runs.
939: - **At `PreInvocation`**, the hook checks the latest reasoning in the transcript tail. A match queues a ≤ 300-token alert for this invocation. This catches plans that haven't turned into a tool call yet.

943: - At `PreInvocation`, if new reasoning mentions an entity with `ruled-out` claims and tier 1 didn't fire, the hook spools a request.
944: - The next tick asks a small model whether the plan is substantively the same as a ruled-out approach. It batches all pending requests into one call.
945: - On a match, it writes an alert to `alerts/<conversation-id>/`. The next `PreInvocation` delivers it: "You're about to retry X. It failed on <date> because Y (clm-…)."

965: ### 7.8 Performance
966: 
967: Antigravity hooks run synchronously and block the agent loop, and `PreInvocation` runs before *every* model call. Latency therefore adds up: at 100 ms per call, a session with 300 model calls gains 30 s.
968: 
969: - **Delivery hook fast path.** Check the conversation's `alerts/` directory and read the transcript from the last cursor (tail only). If nothing new matches, exit. Target: p95 ≤ 60 ms, p50 ≤ 30 ms.
970: - **Delivery hook with injection.** Local SQLite read-only queries plus formatting. Target: p95 ≤ 150 ms.
971: - **Implementation.** Hooks run the compiled Go binary (§18), so start-up costs milliseconds. E5 confirms the fast-path budget on macOS and Windows.
972: - **Measurement.** Cumulative hook time per session is recorded (§10.4) and reported against a session budget (default ≤ 2% of wall-clock time).
973: - **Failure behaviour.** No LLM calls and no network in hooks. If the index is missing or locked, the hook exits with an empty injection. Memory must never block or break work.

Spooled work waits for the next tick. |
